name: Pope Pius IX
role: Pope (1846–1878) and last sovereign of the Papal States
summary: Pius IX began his reign with reforms and an amnesty but after 1848 became a firm opponent of liberalism, nationalism and socialism. His Syllabus of Errors and Quanta Cura condemned religious liberty, state control of schools, civil marriage and divorce, and he held the Papal States' temporal power until Italy took Rome in 1870.

sources.title: The Syllabus of Errors (8 December 1864), Papal Encyclicals Online
sources.author: Pope Pius IX
sources.usedFor: The 80 propositions he condemned on the Church, state, schools, marriage, religious liberty, non-intervention and modern liberalism.

sources.title: Quanta Cura (encyclical, 8 December 1864), Papal Encyclicals Online
sources.author: Pope Pius IX
sources.usedFor: His condemnation of liberty of conscience and the press, popular will as supreme law, state control of schools and socialism; natural law in all hearts.

sources.title: Nostis et Nobiscum (encyclical, 8 December 1849), Papal Encyclicals Online
sources.author: Pope Pius IX
sources.usedFor: His condemnation of socialism and communism, defence of property, natural inequality, obedience to authority, and family order.

sources.title: Pius IX, Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.author: Britannica
sources.usedFor: The record: the 1848 constitution, flight and unconditional restoration in 1850, no constitutional government afterwards, hostility to Italian national sentiment, refusal of the 1870 settlement.

sources.title: Respicientes ea (encyclical on the seizure of the Papal States, 1 November 1870), Papal Encyclicals Online
sources.author: Pope Pius IX
sources.usedFor: His rejection of the Piedmontese seizure of Rome and the plebiscites, defence of temporal power, his army.

sources.title: Ubi nos (encyclical on the Papal States and the Law of Guarantees, 15 May 1871), Papal Encyclicals Online
sources.author: Pope Pius IX
sources.usedFor: His refusal of the guarantees, the claim that papal authority comes directly from God, necessity of civil rule.

all-land-state-owned.rationale: Nostis et Nobiscum condemns taking property for common use and the socialists' theories on it.

annexed-territory-occupation.rationale: He calls the seizure of Rome and the provinces an invasion and occupation and says the people's true feelings were not free to show, but never states a general rule.

arm-foreign-insurgents.rationale: He condemns Piedmont for stirring up rebellion in his provinces with propaganda, conspirators, arms and money.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: The 1848 constitution gave parliament full fiscal powers subject to his veto, but constitutional government was never restored after 1850.

civil-marriage.rationale: The Syllabus condemns the proposition that a real marriage between Christians can exist by a merely civil contract.

clerical-rule.rationale: The Syllabus condemns the proposition that the clergy and the Roman pontiff must be excluded from all dominion over temporal affairs; he himself ruled the Papal States.

consent-of-governed.rationale: He returned to rule without any undertaking of constitutional government after a constituent assembly had ended papal rule; he had also granted a constitution in 1848 under pressure.

democracy-best.rationale: He restored papal rule unconditionally in 1850, never restored the constitution, and refused any restriction on his power.

disputed-territory-plebiscite.rationale: He calls the plebiscites in the Papal provinces and Rome feigned and ludicrous, and denies that a vote could make the seizure legitimate.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Quanta Cura condemns the claim that the people's will is a supreme law free from divine control, and Nostis et Nobiscum cites scripture that rulers are sent by God and to be obeyed for God's sake.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: The Syllabus condemns abolishing the separate clerical courts and the clergy's immunity, so he upheld unequal legal status.

equal-outcomes.rationale: Nostis et Nobiscum says it is a natural and immutable condition that some surpass others in endowments and riches, so equality can never justify usurping others' goods.

force-to-prevent-secession.rationale: He describes his army fighting to hold the provinces and resisting the 1867 attack, though he also relied on French troops.

foreign-policy-non-interference.rationale: The Syllabus condemns the proposition that the principle of non-intervention should be proclaimed and observed.

head-commands-forces.rationale: He speaks of 'Our army' and 'Our soldiers' as sovereign of the Papal States.

land-redistribution.rationale: Nostis et Nobiscum condemns those who claim that the property of others can be taken and divided.

more-religion-public.rationale: Quanta Cura condemns removing religion from public society and holds that kingdoms rest on the Catholic faith.

national-church-status.rationale: The Syllabus condemns the proposition that it is no longer expedient for the Catholic religion to be the only religion of the State.

national-self-determination.rationale: To all expressions of Italian national sentiment the papacy proved hostile and he stood as a barrier to Italian unification.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Quanta Cura teaches that royal power was given not only to govern but most of all to protect the Church.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: Nostis et Nobiscum teaches that members of a society are obliged to obey its lawfully established authority.

no-fault-divorce.rationale: The Syllabus condemns the propositions that marriage is not indissoluble and that civil authority may decree divorce.

no-land-for-peace.rationale: He refused the king's offer to give up the temporal power peacefully, comparing himself to Naboth who would not surrender his inheritance, and refused the Law of Guarantees.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: The Syllabus condemns schools freed from church authority and education unconnected with Catholic faith.

political-violence-legitimate.rationale: The Syllabus condemns rebellion against legitimate princes as lawful.

property-fundamental.rationale: Nostis et Nobiscum condemns taking and dividing the property of others and says equality or liberty never justify injuring others' goods or rights.

public-ownership.rationale: He condemns socialism and communism as plots to overturn the order of human affairs and take property to be divided.

reason-over-faith.rationale: The Syllabus condemns the propositions that human reason alone is arbiter of truth and that reason is the ultimate standard for all truths including religion.

recognize-territorial-claims-from-conque.rationale: He denounces the Piedmontese seizure of his provinces and Rome by force as contrary to divine law and says a plebiscite cannot legitimise the robbery.

reinterpret-religion.rationale: The Syllabus condemns the proposition that revelation is imperfect and subject to progress, and that the Pontiff should come to terms with progress and modern civilization.

religion-illusion.rationale: He teaches the poor that the Catholic religion is the real source of their consolation and of the benefits of Christ's teaching.

religions-one-truth.rationale: The Syllabus condemns the propositions that every religion can lead to salvation and that Protestantism pleases God equally with the Catholic Church.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: He condemns rebellion against legitimate princes and teaches obedience, but never addresses rulers who violate a constitution.

return-lost-territory.rationale: He protested the loss of his provinces and Rome as usurpation, declared the usurpers censured, and refused any agreement accepting the loss.

revolution-legitimate.rationale: The Syllabus condemns the proposition that it is lawful to refuse obedience to legitimate princes and to rebel against them.

right-to-secede.rationale: He calls the 1859 revolt in Emilia a rebellion stirred up by Piedmont and the provinces torn from his rule.

second-chamber.rationale: In 1848 he granted a constitution with a two-chamber parliament, though under pressure and never restored after 1850.

separate-church-state.rationale: He ruled the Papal States as sovereign until 1870, refusing any restriction on his temporal power, and held it indispensable to protect the Church's spiritual power.

shared-marital-authority.rationale: Nostis et Nobiscum says Christian law subjects wives to their husbands and places husbands over their wives.

spiritual-nature.rationale: Quanta Cura wants the Church's salutary influence over nations and princes and royal power used above all to protect the Church.

state-harmful.rationale: Nostis et Nobiscum teaches obedience to lawfully established authority as a divine precept.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: The Syllabus condemns the propositions that the civil power defines the Church's rights, that civil law prevails over the Church's, and that church authority needs government permission.

total-state.rationale: The Syllabus condemns the proposition that the State is the source of all rights with a right not circumscribed by any limits.

traditional-family.rationale: Quanta Cura and Nostis et Nobiscum defend the family's order and parents' rights against the state and socialism.

universal-morality.rationale: Quanta Cura appeals to the eternal natural law engraven by God in all men's hearts.

wife-divorce-without-consent.rationale: The Syllabus condemns divorce by civil authority and the denial that the marriage tie is indissoluble.

worker-ownership.rationale: He condemns socialism and communism, whose aim is to take and divide property among workers and others.

notes: Positions rest on his own encyclicals and the Syllabus (condemned propositions read as his rejection of them) and on Britannica's account of his record. Themes with little recorded: economy beyond property and socialism, justice, environment, technology, foreign alliances and trade.
